# Page: mmCIF Processing

# mmCIF Processing

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [tests/data/test_get_data.py](tests/data/test_get_data.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This document describes the mmCIF (macromolecular Crystallographic Information File) processing system within the PINDER data generation pipeline. The mmCIF processing module is responsible for parsing raw structure files downloaded from RCSB PDB, generating biological assemblies, extracting entity information, identifying interacting chains, and producing structured output files for downstream dataset construction.

The mmCIF processing system is located in the `pinder.data.get_data` module and is a critical component of the dataset generation workflow. For information about how mmCIF files are acquired from RCSB, see [Data Acquisition from RCSB](#5.1). For details on task orchestration and parallel processing, see [Task Orchestration](#5.2). For information about GraphQL-based annotation fetching, see [RCSB Annotations](#5.4).

---

## mmCIF Processing Pipeline Overview

The following diagram shows the complete mmCIF processing pipeline, from input files to structured output:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input Files"
        MMCIF["mmCIF File<br/>pdb_{pdb_id}_xyz-enrich.cif.gz"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Processing Steps"
        READ["read_mmcif_file()<br/>Parse mmCIF format"]
        BIO_ASM["generate_bio_assembly()<br/>Create biological assembly"]
        ENTITIES["get_entities()<br/>Extract entity info"]
        SEQ_MAP["sequence_mapping()<br/>Map PDB to UniProt"]
        CHAINS["get_structure_chains()<br/>Identify chains"]
        INTERACT["get_interacting_chains()<br/>Contact analysis"]
        META["get_metadata()<br/>Extract metadata"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing Functions"
        FILTER["filter_amino_acids()<br/>Protein-only filtering"]
        UNIPROT["infer_uniprot_from_mapping()<br/>Determine UniProt ID"]
        SASA["Buried SASA calculation<br/>Interface analysis"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Files"
        ASSEMBLY_CIF["{pdb_id}-assembly.cif<br/>Biological assembly"]
        METADATA_TSV["{pdb_id}-metadata.tsv<br/>Structure metadata"]
        ENTITY_MAP["Entity mapping DataFrame<br/>chain_id → entity_id"]
        INTERACTION_DF["Interacting chains DataFrame<br/>Contact residues & SASA"]
    end
    
    MMCIF --> READ
    READ --> BIO_ASM
    READ --> META
    
    BIO_ASM --> FILTER
    BIO_ASM --> ENTITIES
    BIO_ASM --> ASSEMBLY_CIF
    
    FILTER --> CHAINS
    ENTITIES --> SEQ_MAP
    SEQ_MAP --> UNIPROT
    
    CHAINS --> INTERACT
    UNIPROT --> INTERACT
    
    INTERACT --> SASA
    SASA --> INTERACTION_DF
    
    META --> METADATA_TSV
    BIO_ASM --> ENTITY_MAP
    
    style READ fill:#e1f5ff
    style BIO_ASM fill:#fff4e1
    style INTERACT fill:#ffe1f5
    style ASSEMBLY_CIF fill:#e1ffe1
```

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:217-240](), [tests/data/test_get_data.py:242-267](), [tests/data/test_get_data.py:348-362]()

---

## Reading and Parsing mmCIF Files

The `read_mmcif_file()` function parses compressed mmCIF files downloaded from RCSB PDB. These files follow the naming convention `pdb_{pdb_id}_xyz-enrich.cif.gz` and contain the complete structural information including atomic coordinates, metadata, and biological assembly instructions.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Input Format"
        GZ_CIF["pdb_00007cm8_xyz-enrich.cif.gz<br/>Compressed mmCIF"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parsing Process"
        READ_FUNC["read_mmcif_file()<br/>Decompress & parse"]
        PDBX["CIFFile object<br/>biotite.structure.io.pdbx"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Extracted Data"
        ATOMS["Atomic coordinates<br/>xyz positions"]
        CHAINS["Chain information<br/>asym_id mapping"]
        ASSEMBLY["Assembly instructions<br/>Transformations"]
        METADATA["Structure metadata<br/>Resolution, method, date"]
    end
    
    GZ_CIF --> READ_FUNC
    READ_FUNC --> PDBX
    PDBX --> ATOMS
    PDBX --> CHAINS
    PDBX --> ASSEMBLY
    PDBX --> METADATA
    
    style READ_FUNC fill:#e1f5ff
    style PDBX fill:#fff4e1
```

The `CIFFile` object from biotite provides access to all mmCIF data categories, including `_atom_site`, `_pdbx_struct_assembly`, `_entity_poly`, and others.

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:114](), [tests/data/test_get_data.py:168]()

---

## Biological Assembly Generation

The `generate_bio_assembly()` function transforms the asymmetric unit structure into the biologically relevant assembly using transformation matrices defined in the mmCIF file. This step is critical because crystallographic structures may contain only a portion of the functional biological unit.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input"
        ASYMMETRIC["Asymmetric Unit<br/>Original mmCIF structure"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Assembly Generation"
        PARSE_ASSEMBLY["Parse assembly instructions<br/>_pdbx_struct_assembly"]
        APPLY_TRANSFORM["Apply transformation matrices<br/>Rotation + translation"]
        CHAIN_RENAME["Rename chains<br/>asym_id → chain_id (e.g., A1, A2)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Entity Mapping"
        BUILD_MAP["Build entity mapping<br/>chain_id → entity_id"]
        ASYM_MAP["Track asym_id<br/>Original chain identifier"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        BIO_ASSEMBLY["AtomArray<br/>Biological assembly structure"]
        ENTITY_DF["Entity mapping DataFrame<br/>chain_id, asym_id, entity_id"]
    end
    
    ASYMMETRIC --> PARSE_ASSEMBLY
    PARSE_ASSEMBLY --> APPLY_TRANSFORM
    APPLY_TRANSFORM --> CHAIN_RENAME
    CHAIN_RENAME --> BUILD_MAP
    CHAIN_RENAME --> BIO_ASSEMBLY
    BUILD_MAP --> ASYM_MAP
    ASYM_MAP --> ENTITY_DF
    
    style APPLY_TRANSFORM fill:#fff4e1
    style BIO_ASSEMBLY fill:#e1ffe1
    style ENTITY_DF fill:#e1f5ff
```

The generated biological assembly may contain significantly more or fewer chains than the asymmetric unit. For example:
- PDB 7KMX: 14 asym_id chains expand to 840 assembly chains
- PDB 7BDU: 7 asym_id chains remain as 7 assembly chains
- PDB 2A79: 13 asym_id chains expand to 34 assembly chains

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:348-362](), [tests/data/test_get_data.py:116]()

---

## Entity Extraction and Sequence Mapping

Entity extraction identifies distinct molecular entities (proteins) within the structure and maps them to their sequences and UniProt accessions.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Entity Identification"
        GET_ENT["get_entities(pdbx_file, entry_id)<br/>Extract from _entity_poly"]
        ENT_DF["Entity DataFrame<br/>entity_id, asym_id, pdb_strand_id"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Sequence Mapping"
        SEQ_MAP["sequence_mapping(pdbx_file, entity_id)<br/>PDB to UniProt mapping"]
        RES_MAP["Residue-level mapping<br/>pdb_num → uniprot_num"]
        RESOLVE["Track resolved residues<br/>Missing vs present"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Chain Association"
        ITER_ASYM["Iterate asym_id values<br/>For each entity"]
        MATCH_CHAIN["Match to assembly chains<br/>asym_id prefix matching"]
        UNIPROT["infer_uniprot_from_mapping()<br/>Determine UniProt accession"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        CHAIN_MAP["chain_mapping Dictionary<br/>chain → mapping DataFrame"]
        ENRICHED_ENT["Enriched entity DataFrame<br/>+ chain, uniprot, length_resolved"]
    end
    
    GET_ENT --> ENT_DF
    ENT_DF --> SEQ_MAP
    SEQ_MAP --> RES_MAP
    RES_MAP --> RESOLVE
    
    ENT_DF --> ITER_ASYM
    ITER_ASYM --> MATCH_CHAIN
    RES_MAP --> UNIPROT
    
    MATCH_CHAIN --> CHAIN_MAP
    UNIPROT --> ENRICHED_ENT
    RESOLVE --> ENRICHED_ENT
    
    style SEQ_MAP fill:#fff4e1
    style UNIPROT fill:#e1f5ff
    style ENRICHED_ENT fill:#e1ffe1
```

The sequence mapping process creates a residue-by-residue correspondence between PDB numbering and UniProt canonical sequences, tracking which residues are structurally resolved. This is essential for later alignment and superposition operations.

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:118-149]()

---

## Interacting Chain Identification

The `get_interacting_chains()` function performs contact analysis to identify which chain pairs form protein-protein interfaces. This is a core step in determining which structures qualify for inclusion in the PINDER dataset.

### Contact Detection Algorithm

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input"
        BIO_ASM["Biological assembly<br/>AtomArray"]
        ENTITIES["Entity DataFrame<br/>Chain metadata"]
        PARAMS["Parameters<br/>contact_threshold (5Å)<br/>backbone_only (False)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Atom Selection"
        FILTER_TYPE["Filter by atom type<br/>CA only if backbone_only"]
        CHAIN_PAIRS["Generate chain pairs<br/>All unique combinations"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Distance Calculation"
        DIST_CALC["Calculate pairwise distances<br/>Between chain atoms"]
        THRESHOLD["Apply threshold<br/>distances ≤ contact_threshold"]
        COUNT_PAIRS["Count atom pairs<br/>Below threshold"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Residue Analysis"
        MAP_RES["Map atoms to residues<br/>Unique residue IDs"]
        COUNT_RES_PAIRS["Count residue pairs<br/>In contact"]
        TOTAL_RES["Count total residues<br/>In interface"]
        RES_LIST["List contacting residues<br/>Comma-separated"]
    end
    
    subgraph "SASA Calculation"
        CALC_SASA["Calculate buried SASA<br/>Interface area"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        INTERACT_DF["Interacting chains DataFrame<br/>chain_1, chain_2, asym_id_1, asym_id_2<br/>n_residue_pairs, n_residues<br/>buried_sasa, residue lists"]
    end
    
    BIO_ASM --> FILTER_TYPE
    ENTITIES --> CHAIN_PAIRS
    PARAMS --> FILTER_TYPE
    
    FILTER_TYPE --> DIST_CALC
    CHAIN_PAIRS --> DIST_CALC
    PARAMS --> THRESHOLD
    
    DIST_CALC --> THRESHOLD
    THRESHOLD --> COUNT_PAIRS
    COUNT_PAIRS --> MAP_RES
    
    MAP_RES --> COUNT_RES_PAIRS
    MAP_RES --> TOTAL_RES
    MAP_RES --> RES_LIST
    
    COUNT_RES_PAIRS --> INTERACT_DF
    TOTAL_RES --> INTERACT_DF
    RES_LIST --> INTERACT_DF
    
    BIO_ASM --> CALC_SASA
    CALC_SASA --> INTERACT_DF
    
    style DIST_CALC fill:#fff4e1
    style CALC_SASA fill:#e1f5ff
    style INTERACT_DF fill:#e1ffe1
```

### Contact Analysis Output

The `get_interacting_chains()` function returns a DataFrame with the following fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `chain_1` | First chain identifier from assembly |
| `chain_2` | Second chain identifier from assembly |
| `asym_id_1` | Asymmetric unit ID for chain 1 |
| `asym_id_2` | Asymmetric unit ID for chain 2 |
| `pdb_strand_id_1` | Author chain ID for chain 1 |
| `pdb_strand_id_2` | Author chain ID for chain 2 |
| `entry_id` | PDB ID |
| `n_residue_pairs` | Number of residue pairs in contact |
| `n_residues` | Total unique residues in interface |
| `buried_sasa` | Buried solvent accessible surface area (Ų) |
| `chain_1_residues` | Comma-separated list of contacting residue numbers |
| `chain_2_residues` | Comma-separated list of contacting residue numbers |

### Parameter Effects

The contact detection behavior varies based on parameters:

| `contact_threshold` | `backbone_only` | Effect |
|---------------------|-----------------|--------|
| 5.0 Å | False | Default configuration - all heavy atoms, tight contacts |
| 10.0 Å | False | Expanded interface - captures more distant interactions |
| 5.0 Å | True | Backbone only - Cα atoms, stricter interface definition |
| 10.0 Å | True | Relaxed backbone - broader interface region |

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:40-91](), [tests/data/test_get_data.py:93-163]()

---

## Metadata Extraction

The `get_metadata()` function extracts structural and experimental metadata from the mmCIF file that characterizes the quality and type of the structure.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "mmCIF Categories"
        EXPTL["_exptl<br/>Experimental method"]
        REFINE["_refine<br/>Resolution"]
        DATES["_pdbx_database_status<br/>Dates"]
        ASSEMBLY_META["_pdbx_struct_assembly<br/>Assembly info"]
        OLIGO["_pdbx_struct_assembly_prop<br/>Oligomeric state"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Extracted Fields"
        METHOD["method<br/>X-RAY DIFFRACTION, etc."]
        RES["resolution<br/>Angstroms"]
        DATE["date, release_date<br/>YYYY-MM-DD"]
        ASM_DETAILS["assembly_details<br/>Assembly type"]
        OLIGO_STATE["oligomeric_details<br/>oligomeric_count"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        META_DF["Metadata DataFrame<br/>Single row per structure"]
    end
    
    EXPTL --> METHOD
    REFINE --> RES
    DATES --> DATE
    ASSEMBLY_META --> ASM_DETAILS
    OLIGO --> OLIGO_STATE
    
    METHOD --> META_DF
    RES --> META_DF
    DATE --> META_DF
    ASM_DETAILS --> META_DF
    OLIGO_STATE --> META_DF
    
    style META_DF fill:#e1ffe1
```

Example metadata record:

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| `entry_id` | 7CM8 |
| `method` | X-RAY DIFFRACTION |
| `date` | 2020-07-25 |
| `release_date` | 2020-08-19 |
| `resolution` | 1.90 |
| `assembly` | 1 |
| `assembly_details` | author_and_software_defined_assembly |
| `oligomeric_details` | dimeric |
| `oligomeric_count` | 2 |

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:165-189](), [tests/data/test_get_data.py:191-216]()

---

## Main Processing Function

The `process_mmcif()` function orchestrates the complete processing pipeline, coordinating all the steps described above.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input"
        MMCIF_PATH["Path to mmCIF file<br/>pdb_{pdb_id}_xyz-enrich.cif.gz"]
    end
    
    subgraph "process_mmcif() Workflow"
        EXTRACT_ID["Extract pdb_id<br/>From filename"]
        READ["read_mmcif_file()<br/>Load mmCIF"]
        GEN_ASM["generate_bio_assembly()<br/>Create assembly & mapping"]
        GET_META["get_metadata()<br/>Extract metadata"]
        FILTER_AA["filter_amino_acids()<br/>Protein-only"]
        GET_ENT["get_entities()<br/>Entity information"]
        GET_CHAINS["get_structure_chains()<br/>Chain identifiers"]
        SEQ_MAPPING["sequence_mapping()<br/>Per entity & asym_id"]
        INFER_UNIPROT["infer_uniprot_from_mapping()<br/>UniProt accession"]
        BUILD_CHAIN_MAP["Build chain_mapping dict<br/>Chain → mapping"]
        GET_INTERACT["get_interacting_chains()<br/>Contact analysis"]
        CLASSIFY["Classify complex_type<br/>homomer vs heteromer"]
        SET_STATUS["Set status<br/>complete/incomplete"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Files"
        ASSEMBLY_OUT["{pdb_id}-assembly.cif<br/>Biological assembly"]
        METADATA_OUT["{pdb_id}-metadata.tsv<br/>Structure metadata"]
        CHAINS_OUT["Optional: Chain-level data<br/>For downstream processing"]
    end
    
    MMCIF_PATH --> EXTRACT_ID
    EXTRACT_ID --> READ
    READ --> GEN_ASM
    READ --> GET_META
    GEN_ASM --> FILTER_AA
    GEN_ASM --> ASSEMBLY_OUT
    FILTER_AA --> GET_ENT
    FILTER_AA --> GET_CHAINS
    GET_ENT --> SEQ_MAPPING
    SEQ_MAPPING --> INFER_UNIPROT
    GET_CHAINS --> BUILD_CHAIN_MAP
    INFER_UNIPROT --> BUILD_CHAIN_MAP
    BUILD_CHAIN_MAP --> GET_INTERACT
    GET_INTERACT --> CLASSIFY
    GET_META --> CLASSIFY
    CLASSIFY --> SET_STATUS
    SET_STATUS --> METADATA_OUT
    BUILD_CHAIN_MAP --> CHAINS_OUT
    
    style process_mmcif fill:#fff4e1
    style ASSEMBLY_OUT fill:#e1ffe1
    style METADATA_OUT fill:#e1ffe1
```

The `process_mmcif()` function enriches the metadata with derived fields:

- `complex_type`: Determined by comparing UniProt accessions - "homomer" if all chains have the same UniProt ID, "heteromer" otherwise
- `status`: Set to "complete" if processing succeeds without errors, otherwise may indicate issues

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:217-240]()

---

## Output File Formats

### Assembly CIF File

The `{pdb_id}-assembly.cif` file contains the biological assembly with renamed chain identifiers. Chains are named using a prefix system where the asym_id from the asymmetric unit is preserved with numeric suffixes (e.g., `A1`, `A2` for multiple copies of asym_id `A`).

**Chain naming example for PDB 7CM8:**
```
Asymmetric unit:    A
Biological assembly: A1, A2  (dimer)
```

The assembly CIF can be converted to PDB format with specific chain selections using the `atoms.cif_to_pdb()` function.

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:242-267]()

### Metadata TSV File

The `{pdb_id}-metadata.tsv` file is a tab-separated values file containing a single row with the metadata fields extracted by `get_metadata()` plus derived fields from `process_mmcif()`:

```
entry_id    method    date    release_date    resolution    assembly    ...
7cm8        X-RAY...  2020... 2020-08-19     1.9           1          ...
```

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:227-236]()

---

## Special Cases and Edge Cases

### Large Oligomeric Assemblies

Some structures produce extremely large biological assemblies:

| PDB ID | Asym IDs | Assembly Chains | Entity IDs |
|--------|----------|-----------------|------------|
| 7KMX | 14 | 840 | 2 |
| 6RW4 | 125 | 125 | 42 |
| 2Y26 | 40 | 120 | 2 |

These structures require significant memory and processing time during contact analysis.

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:284-362]()

### Monomer Processing

Structures containing only a single protein chain are processed but may not produce interacting chain data since no protein-protein interface exists. The `process_mmcif()` function handles these cases gracefully.

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:364-368]()

### Invalid or Incomplete Structures

Some mmCIF files may lack required data or contain invalid structures. The `process_mmcif()` function may raise exceptions for these cases, which are caught during task orchestration to skip problematic entries.

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:237-240]()

---

## Integration with Dataset Pipeline

The mmCIF processing outputs feed directly into the dataset construction workflow:

1. **Assembly CIF files** are used to create monomer structures (receptor/ligand) by extracting individual chains
2. **Metadata TSV files** provide filtering criteria (resolution, method, oligomeric state)
3. **Entity mappings** enable pairing of apo structures with holo complexes based on UniProt accessions
4. **Interacting chain data** defines which chain pairs constitute valid protein-protein interfaces for the dataset

The processed data is organized in the file system by two-character PDB codes (e.g., `cm/pdb_00007cm8/`) and subsequently indexed for efficient access by the data loading system (see [PinderLoader](#4.1)).

**Sources:** [tests/data/test_get_data.py:1-368]()

---

# Page: RCSB Annotations

# RCSB Annotations

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/pinder-data/pinder/data/pipeline/tasks.py](src/pinder-data/pinder/data/pipeline/tasks.py)
- [tests/data/test_graphql.py](tests/data/test_graphql.py)
- [tests/data/test_tasks.py](tests/data/test_tasks.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This document describes the GraphQL-based annotation system that fetches structural and functional metadata from the RCSB PDB database. The annotation pipeline retrieves Pfam domains, ECOD/SCOP/CATH structural classifications, sequence features, and enzyme commission (EC) numbers for protein entries.

For information about downloading raw structure files from RCSB, see [Data Acquisition from RCSB](#5.1). For details on how annotation tasks are orchestrated within the broader pipeline, see [Task Orchestration](#5.2).

## Overview

The RCSB annotation system queries the RCSB PDB GraphQL API to enrich structural data with biological annotations. These annotations are essential for understanding protein domain composition, structural classifications, and functional properties that inform dataset filtering and analysis.

The system processes PDB IDs in parallel batches, fetching comprehensive annotation data and organizing it into structured CSV files for downstream use.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input"
        PDB_IDS["PDB ID List<br/>pdb_id_glob()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "GraphQL Fetching"
        FETCH["fetch_entry_annotations()<br/>Per-PDB GraphQL query"]
        CACHE["JSON Cache<br/>{pdb_id}.json"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parsing"
        PARSE["parse_annotation_data()<br/>JSON to DataFrames"]
        PFAM_DF["Pfam DataFrame<br/>19 columns"]
        FEAT_DF["Features DataFrame<br/>14 columns"]
        ANNOT_DF["Annotations DataFrame<br/>12 columns"]
        EC_DF["EC DataFrame"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parallel Processing"
        POPULATE["populate_rcsb_annotations()<br/>concurrent.futures"]
        WORKERS["max_workers<br/>Parallel execution"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Storage"
        PFAM_CSV["pfam/{pdb_id}.csv.gz"]
        FEAT_CSV["features/{pdb_id}.csv.gz"]
        ANNOT_CSV["annotations/{pdb_id}.csv.gz"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Collection"
        COLLECT["collect_rcsb_annotations()<br/>Aggregate all PDB entries"]
        PFAM_AGG["pfam.csv.gz"]
        ANNOT_ECOD["annotations_ecod.csv.gz"]
        ANNOT_SCOP["annotations_scop.csv.gz"]
        ANNOT_CATH["annotations_cath.csv.gz"]
        FEAT_ECOD["features_ecod.csv.gz"]
        FEAT_SCOP["features_scop.csv.gz"]
        FEAT_CATH["features_cath.csv.gz"]
    end
    
    PDB_IDS --> POPULATE
    POPULATE --> WORKERS
    WORKERS --> FETCH
    FETCH --> CACHE
    CACHE --> PARSE
    
    PARSE --> PFAM_DF
    PARSE --> FEAT_DF
    PARSE --> ANNOT_DF
    PARSE --> EC_DF
    
    PFAM_DF --> PFAM_CSV
    FEAT_DF --> FEAT_CSV
    ANNOT_DF --> ANNOT_CSV
    
    PFAM_CSV --> COLLECT
    FEAT_CSV --> COLLECT
    ANNOT_CSV --> COLLECT
    
    COLLECT --> PFAM_AGG
    COLLECT --> ANNOT_ECOD
    COLLECT --> ANNOT_SCOP
    COLLECT --> ANNOT_CATH
    COLLECT --> FEAT_ECOD
    COLLECT --> FEAT_SCOP
    COLLECT --> FEAT_CATH
```

**Annotation Pipeline Architecture**

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:1-100](), [src/pinder-data/pinder/data/pipeline/tasks.py:44-47]()

## GraphQL API Integration

The annotation system interfaces with the RCSB PDB GraphQL API to retrieve structured metadata. The `fetch_entry_annotations()` function executes GraphQL queries for individual PDB entries and caches responses locally.

### Fetching Process

The fetching mechanism retrieves comprehensive annotation data for each PDB entry:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "fetch_entry_annotations"
        INPUT["pdb_id: str<br/>data_json: Path<br/>use_cache: bool"]
        CHECK["Check cache<br/>data_json.is_file()"]
        QUERY["Execute GraphQL<br/>RCSB PDB API"]
        WRITE["Write JSON<br/>{pdb_id}.json"]
    end
    
    INPUT --> CHECK
    CHECK -->|"Cache miss"| QUERY
    CHECK -->|"use_cache=True"| RETURN["Return cached"]
    QUERY --> WRITE
    WRITE --> RETURN
```

**Fetch Entry Annotations Flow**

The function supports caching to avoid redundant API calls. When `use_cache=True`, it skips fetching if the JSON file already exists.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:47-50]()

## Annotation Types

The GraphQL API returns four distinct types of annotation data, each stored in separate DataFrames:

### Pfam Domain Annotations

Pfam annotations describe protein domain families and provide functional classification. The Pfam DataFrame contains 19 columns including:

| Key Fields | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| `rcsb_id` | Pfam accession (e.g., PF00076, PF14939) |
| `rcsb_pfam_identifier` | Pfam family name (e.g., RRM_1, CPSF_A) |
| Positional data | Start/end positions of domain boundaries |
| Asymmetric chain IDs | Chain associations |

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:51-60]()

### Structural Classification Annotations

The annotations DataFrame contains hierarchical structural classifications from ECOD, SCOP, and CATH databases. It has 12 columns and includes annotation IDs such as:

| Database | Example IDs |
|----------|-------------|
| CATH | 3.30.70.330 |
| ECOD | 8051194, 8061923, 8052530 |
| SCOP | e6q0rA1, e6q0rA2, e6q0rA3, e6q0rD1, d6q0rd1, d6q0rd2 |

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:13-38](), [tests/data/test_graphql.py:63]()

### Sequence Feature Annotations

The features DataFrame captures 14 columns of sequence-level annotations including:

| Feature Type | Description |
|--------------|-------------|
| `ASA` | Accessible surface area |
| `HELIX_P` | Alpha helix secondary structure |
| `SHEET` | Beta sheet secondary structure |
| `UNASSIGNED_SEC_STRUCT` | Unassigned secondary structure |
| `SCOP`, `SCOP2B_SUPERFAMILY` | SCOP classifications |
| `CATH`, `ECOD` | Structural domain features |
| `BINDING_SITE` | Ligand binding sites |
| `CIS-PEPTIDE` | Cis-peptide bonds |
| `UNOBSERVED_RESIDUE_XYZ` | Missing residues |
| `UNOBSERVED_ATOM_XYZ` | Missing atoms |

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:13-26](), [tests/data/test_graphql.py:61-62]()

### Enzyme Commission (EC) Numbers

The EC DataFrame captures enzyme classification data. While not all entries have EC annotations, the DataFrame structure accommodates these when present.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:51](), [tests/data/test_graphql.py:56]()

## Data Parsing

The `parse_annotation_data()` function transforms raw JSON responses into structured DataFrames:

```mermaid
graph TD
    JSON["JSON Response<br/>{pdb_id}.json"]
    PARSER["parse_annotation_data()"]
    
    PFAM["pfam_df<br/>19 columns<br/>Domain families"]
    FEAT["feature_df<br/>14 columns<br/>Sequence features"]
    ANNOT["annotation_df<br/>12 columns<br/>Structural classifications"]
    EC["ec_df<br/>Enzyme classifications"]
    
    JSON --> PARSER
    PARSER --> PFAM
    PARSER --> FEAT
    PARSER --> ANNOT
    PARSER --> EC
```

**Annotation Data Parsing**

The parser extracts different annotation types from the nested GraphQL response structure and normalizes them into tabular formats suitable for downstream analysis.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:51-63]()

## Parallel Processing System

The `populate_rcsb_annotations()` function orchestrates parallel fetching and parsing of annotations across multiple PDB entries:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input Parameters"
        PINDER_DIR["pinder_dir: Path<br/>Output directory"]
        PDB_IDS["pdb_ids: list[str]<br/>Target entries"]
        PARALLEL["parallel: bool<br/>Enable parallelism"]
        WORKERS["max_workers: int<br/>Thread pool size"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Directory Structure"
        BASE["rcsb_annotations/"]
        PFAM_DIR["pfam/"]
        FEAT_DIR["features/"]
        ANNOT_DIR["annotations/"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parallel Execution"
        EXECUTOR["concurrent.futures<br/>ThreadPoolExecutor"]
        TASKS["List[Future]<br/>Per-PDB tasks"]
        FETCH_PARSE["fetch + parse<br/>Per worker"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Files"
        PFAM_OUT["{pdb_id}.csv.gz<br/>In pfam/"]
        FEAT_OUT["{pdb_id}.csv.gz<br/>In features/"]
        ANNOT_OUT["{pdb_id}.csv.gz<br/>In annotations/"]
    end
    
    PINDER_DIR --> BASE
    BASE --> PFAM_DIR
    BASE --> FEAT_DIR
    BASE --> ANNOT_DIR
    
    PDB_IDS --> EXECUTOR
    PARALLEL --> EXECUTOR
    WORKERS --> EXECUTOR
    
    EXECUTOR --> TASKS
    TASKS --> FETCH_PARSE
    
    FETCH_PARSE --> PFAM_OUT
    FETCH_PARSE --> FEAT_OUT
    FETCH_PARSE --> ANNOT_OUT
    
    PFAM_OUT --> PFAM_DIR
    FEAT_OUT --> FEAT_DIR
    ANNOT_OUT --> ANNOT_DIR
```

**Parallel Annotation Population**

The function creates separate subdirectories for each annotation type and writes compressed CSV files for each PDB entry. When `parallel=True`, it uses a thread pool to fetch multiple entries concurrently.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:66-82]()

## Annotation Collection

After individual PDB entries are annotated, the `collect_rcsb_annotations()` function aggregates the per-entry CSV files into unified datasets:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input Directory"
        ANNOT_BASE["rcsb_annotations/"]
        PFAM_FILES["pfam/{pdb_id}.csv.gz<br/>Per-entry files"]
        FEAT_FILES["features/{pdb_id}.csv.gz<br/>Per-entry files"]
        ANNOT_FILES["annotations/{pdb_id}.csv.gz<br/>Per-entry files"]
    end
    
    subgraph "collect_rcsb_annotations"
        COLLECTOR["Aggregate & Filter<br/>By annotation type"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Aggregated Outputs"
        PFAM_AGG["pfam.csv.gz<br/>All Pfam domains"]
        
        subgraph "Annotations by DB"
            ANNOT_ECOD["annotations_ecod.csv.gz"]
            ANNOT_SCOP["annotations_scop.csv.gz"]
            ANNOT_CATH["annotations_cath.csv.gz"]
        end
        
        subgraph "Features by DB"
            FEAT_ECOD["features_ecod.csv.gz"]
            FEAT_SCOP["features_scop.csv.gz"]
            FEAT_CATH["features_cath.csv.gz"]
        end
    end
    
    ANNOT_BASE --> PFAM_FILES
    ANNOT_BASE --> FEAT_FILES
    ANNOT_BASE --> ANNOT_FILES
    
    PFAM_FILES --> COLLECTOR
    FEAT_FILES --> COLLECTOR
    ANNOT_FILES --> COLLECTOR
    
    COLLECTOR --> PFAM_AGG
    COLLECTOR --> ANNOT_ECOD
    COLLECTOR --> ANNOT_SCOP
    COLLECTOR --> ANNOT_CATH
    COLLECTOR --> FEAT_ECOD
    COLLECTOR --> FEAT_SCOP
    COLLECTOR --> FEAT_CATH
```

**Annotation Collection Process**

The collection process reads all per-entry CSV files, filters annotations and features by their respective databases (ECOD, SCOP, CATH), and writes consolidated CSV files. The Pfam annotations are not database-specific and are aggregated into a single file.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:85-99]()

## Task Integration

The annotation fetching integrates with the broader pipeline task system through the `get_rcsb_annotations` step:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Task Configuration"
        STEP["Step: get_rcsb_annotations"]
        INPUT_TYPE["input_type: pdb_ids"]
        CACHE["cache_func: get_rcsb_unannotated"]
        SCATTER["scatter_func: chunk_collection"]
        BATCH["batch_size: 1"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Task Execution"
        GLOB["pdb_id_glob()<br/>Extract PDB IDs"]
        UNANNOTATED["get_rcsb_unannotated()<br/>Filter cached"]
        CHUNK["chunk_collection()<br/>Create batches"]
        TASKS["Task batches<br/>[[pdb_id1], [pdb_id2], ...]"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing"
        RUN["run_task()<br/>Execute batch"]
        POPULATE["populate_rcsb_annotations()<br/>Fetch & parse"]
    end
    
    STEP --> INPUT_TYPE
    INPUT_TYPE --> GLOB
    CACHE --> UNANNOTATED
    
    GLOB --> UNANNOTATED
    UNANNOTATED --> SCATTER
    SCATTER --> CHUNK
    CHUNK --> TASKS
    
    TASKS --> RUN
    RUN --> POPULATE
```

**Task Integration Flow**

The annotation task follows the standard pipeline pattern:
1. **Input gathering**: `pdb_id_glob()` extracts PDB IDs from entry directories
2. **Cache filtering**: `get_rcsb_unannotated()` identifies entries without annotations
3. **Scatter**: `chunk_collection()` divides PDB IDs into batches
4. **Execution**: `run_task()` invokes `populate_rcsb_annotations()` for each batch

Sources: [tests/data/test_tasks.py:56-64](), [src/pinder-data/pinder/data/pipeline/tasks.py:44-47]()

## Directory Structure

The annotation system creates a hierarchical directory structure under `pinder_dir/rcsb_annotations/`:

```
pinder_dir/
└── rcsb_annotations/
    ├── pfam/
    │   ├── 6Q0R.csv.gz
    │   ├── 2A79.csv.gz
    │   └── ...
    ├── features/
    │   ├── 6Q0R.csv.gz
    │   ├── 2A79.csv.gz
    │   └── ...
    ├── annotations/
    │   ├── 6Q0R.csv.gz
    │   ├── 2A79.csv.gz
    │   └── ...
    ├── pfam.csv.gz
    ├── annotations_ecod.csv.gz
    ├── annotations_scop.csv.gz
    ├── annotations_cath.csv.gz
    ├── features_ecod.csv.gz
    ├── features_scop.csv.gz
    └── features_cath.csv.gz
```

Per-entry files are written during the population phase, while aggregated files are created during the collection phase.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:74-82](), [tests/data/test_graphql.py:88-99]()

## Caching Strategy

The annotation system implements two levels of caching:

### JSON Response Caching

The `fetch_entry_annotations()` function caches raw GraphQL responses as JSON files. When `use_cache=True`, it skips API requests for entries with existing cache files.

### Task-Level Caching

The `get_rcsb_unannotated()` cache function (used in task orchestration) identifies PDB entries that lack annotation CSV files, preventing redundant fetching of already-processed entries.

This dual-caching approach optimizes both API usage and processing time, particularly important when re-running pipeline stages after failures or when adding new PDB entries to an existing dataset.

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:49](), [tests/data/test_tasks.py:59-60]()

## Key Functions Reference

| Function | Module | Purpose |
|----------|--------|---------|
| `fetch_entry_annotations()` | `pinder.data.annotation.graphql` | Fetch GraphQL data for single PDB entry |
| `parse_annotation_data()` | `pinder.data.annotation.graphql` | Parse JSON into DataFrames |
| `populate_rcsb_annotations()` | `pinder.data.annotation.graphql` | Parallel annotation fetching |
| `collect_rcsb_annotations()` | `pinder.data.annotation.graphql` | Aggregate per-entry CSVs |
| `pdb_id_glob()` | `pinder.data.pipeline.tasks` | Extract PDB IDs from directories |
| `get_rcsb_unannotated()` | `pinder.data.pipeline.cache` | Filter unannotated entries |

Sources: [tests/data/test_graphql.py:1-100](), [src/pinder-data/pinder/data/pipeline/tasks.py:44-47]()

# Page: Evaluation

# Evaluation

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page explains the PINDER evaluation system, which provides standardized assessment of protein-protein docking methods against benchmark test sets. The evaluation harness processes predicted structures and computes CAPRI-standard metrics to enable fair comparison across methods.

For detailed information about specific aspects of evaluation:
- For the CLI tool and directory structure, see [Evaluation Harness](#6.1)
- For metric definitions and calculations, see [Metrics](#6.2)
- For test set characteristics and selection, see [Benchmark Test Sets](#6.3)

## Overview

The PINDER evaluation system consists of three main components:

1. **Evaluation Harness**: A CLI tool (`pinder_eval`) and Python API that processes predicted structures
2. **Metrics Engine**: Implementations of CAPRI metrics (iRMS, LRMS, Fnat, DockQ) 
3. **Benchmark Test Sets**: Curated holdout sets (PINDER-XL, PINDER-S, PINDER-AF2) for standardized evaluation

The evaluation workflow follows community-standard CAPRI (Critical Assessment of PRediction of Interactions) guidelines for assessing docking quality.

Sources: [README.md:300-381]()

## System Architecture

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input: Method Predictions"
        EVAL_DIR["eval_dir/"]
        METHOD_DIR["method_name/"]
        SYSTEM_DIR["system_id/"]
        HOLO_DECOYS["holo_decoys/<br/>model_1.pdb..."]
        APO_DECOYS["apo_decoys/<br/>model_1.pdb..."]
        PRED_DECOYS["predicted_decoys/<br/>model_1.pdb..."]
    end
    
    subgraph "PINDER Test Sets"
        INDEX["index.parquet<br/>test split definitions"]
        NATIVE["test_set_pdbs/<br/>native structures"]
        PINDER_XL["PINDER-XL<br/>1955 systems"]
        PINDER_S["PINDER-S<br/>250 systems"]
        PINDER_AF2["PINDER-AF2<br/>180 systems"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Evaluation Engine"
        CLI["pinder_eval CLI"]
        LOADER["System Loader<br/>PinderSystem"]
        METRICS["pinder.eval.dockq<br/>Metric Calculator"]
        METHOD_METRICS["MethodMetrics<br/>Aggregation"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Outputs"
        SYSTEM_CSV["per-system metrics"]
        LEADERBOARD["leaderboard.csv<br/>aggregated results"]
        CAPRI_CLASS["CAPRI classifications"]
    end
    
    EVAL_DIR --> METHOD_DIR
    METHOD_DIR --> SYSTEM_DIR
    SYSTEM_DIR --> HOLO_DECOYS
    SYSTEM_DIR --> APO_DECOYS
    SYSTEM_DIR --> PRED_DECOYS
    
    INDEX --> CLI
    NATIVE --> CLI
    
    PINDER_XL -.-> INDEX
    PINDER_S -.-> INDEX
    PINDER_AF2 -.-> INDEX
    
    CLI --> LOADER
    LOADER --> METRICS
    METRICS --> METHOD_METRICS
    
    METHOD_METRICS --> SYSTEM_CSV
    METHOD_METRICS --> LEADERBOARD
    METHOD_METRICS --> CAPRI_CLASS
    
    style CLI fill:#e1f5ff
    style METRICS fill:#fff4e1
    style METHOD_METRICS fill:#ffe1f5
```

**Description**: The evaluation system takes a standardized directory structure containing method predictions, loads native structures from test sets, computes CAPRI metrics per system, and aggregates results into leaderboard-ready outputs. The `pinder_eval` CLI orchestrates the entire process, using `MethodMetrics` for aggregation logic.

Sources: [README.md:307-381]()

## Evaluation Workflow

```mermaid
graph TD
    START["Start Evaluation"]
    PARSE["Parse eval_dir<br/>Extract method names<br/>and system IDs"]
    
    LOAD_INDEX["Load Index<br/>Filter by split"]
    VALIDATE["Validate Systems<br/>Check completeness"]
    
    PARALLEL["Parallel Processing<br/>multiprocessing pool"]
    
    subgraph "Per-System Evaluation"
        LOAD_NATIVE["Load Native Structure<br/>PinderSystem"]
        LOAD_DECOYS["Load Decoy Models<br/>Parse rank from filename"]
        ALIGN["Align Decoys to Native<br/>Chain matching R/L"]
        COMPUTE["Compute Metrics<br/>iRMS, LRMS, Fnat, DockQ"]
        CLASSIFY["Assign CAPRI Class<br/>Incorrect/Acceptable/Medium/High"]
    end
    
    AGGREGATE["Aggregate Results<br/>MethodMetrics"]
    PENALTY["Apply Missing Penalties<br/>iRMS=100, LRMS=100<br/>Fnat=0, DockQ=0"]
    
    OUTPUT_CSV["Write System CSV"]
    OUTPUT_LEADER["Generate Leaderboard"]
    
    START --> PARSE
    PARSE --> LOAD_INDEX
    LOAD_INDEX --> VALIDATE
    VALIDATE --> PARALLEL
    
    PARALLEL --> LOAD_NATIVE
    LOAD_NATIVE --> LOAD_DECOYS
    LOAD_DECOYS --> ALIGN
    ALIGN --> COMPUTE
    COMPUTE --> CLASSIFY
    
    CLASSIFY --> AGGREGATE
    VALIDATE --> PENALTY
    PENALTY --> AGGREGATE
    
    AGGREGATE --> OUTPUT_CSV
    AGGREGATE --> OUTPUT_LEADER
    
    style PARALLEL fill:#e1f5ff
    style COMPUTE fill:#fff4e1
    style AGGREGATE fill:#ffe1f5
```

**Description**: Evaluation proceeds by parsing the directory structure, loading the appropriate test set index, validating system coverage, and processing each system in parallel. Missing predictions receive penalty scores to ensure fair comparison across incomplete method submissions.

Sources: [README.md:307-327](), [README.md:365-377]()

## Directory Structure Requirements

The evaluation system expects a specific directory layout that separates predictions by method, system, and monomer type:

```
eval_dir/
└── method_name/
    ├── system_id_1/
    │   ├── holo_decoys/
    │   │   ├── model_1.pdb
    │   │   ├── model_2.pdb
    │   │   └── ...
    │   ├── apo_decoys/
    │   │   ├── model_1.pdb
    │   │   └── ...
    │   └── predicted_decoys/
    │       ├── model_1.pdb
    │       └── ...
    └── system_id_2/
        └── ...
```

### Directory Component Requirements

| Component | Description | Required |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| `eval_dir` | Root directory containing one or more methods | Yes |
| `method_name` | Subdirectory for each evaluated method | Yes |
| `system_id` | PINDER system ID (e.g., `1an1__A1_P00761--1an1__B1_P80424`) | Yes |
| `holo_decoys` | Predictions using holo (bound) monomers | Conditional* |
| `apo_decoys` | Predictions using apo (unbound) monomers | Conditional* |
| `predicted_decoys` | Predictions using AF2/predicted monomers | Conditional* |
| `model_<rank>.pdb` | Individual decoy models with extractable rank | Yes |

*At least one monomer type directory must be present per system.

### Decoy Model Requirements

Each decoy PDB file must satisfy:

1. **Chain naming**: Exactly two chains labeled `R` (receptor) and `L` (ligand)
2. **Rank extraction**: Filename must match regex pattern `r"\d+(?=\D*$)"` to extract prediction rank
3. **Structure validity**: Valid PDB format readable by structure parsing utilities

Sources: [README.md:328-363]()

## Command-Line Interface

The `pinder_eval` CLI provides the primary interface for running evaluations:

```bash
pinder_eval --eval_dir <path> \
            --method_name <name> \
            --allow_missing \
            --max_workers <N>
```

### CLI Arguments

| Argument | Short | Description | Default |
|----------|-------|-------------|---------|
| `--eval_dir` | `-f` | Path to evaluation directory | Required |
| `--method_name` | `-m`, `-n` | Optional output CSV prefix | `None` |
| `--serial` | `-s` | Disable parallel processing | `False` |
| `--allow_missing` | `-a` | Permit incomplete system coverage | `False` |
| `--custom_index` | `-c` | Path/URI to custom index file | `None` |
| `--max_workers` | `-w` | Maximum parallel processes | All cores |

### Example Usage

```bash
# Evaluate a single method on PINDER-S
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions \
            --method_name my_method \
            --allow_missing

# Evaluate with custom parallelism
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions \
            --max_workers 8

# Use custom test set definition
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions \
            --custom_index gs://my-bucket/custom_index.parquet
```

Sources: [README.md:307-327]()

## Missing Prediction Penalties

To ensure fair comparison across methods, incomplete submissions receive standardized penalty scores:

| Metric | Penalty Value | Interpretation |
|--------|---------------|----------------|
| `iRMS` | 100.0 | Maximum possible error (Ångströms) |
| `LRMS` | 100.0 | Maximum possible error (Ångströms) |
| `Fnat` | 0.0 | No native contacts recovered |
| `DockQ` | 0.0 | Lowest quality score |
| `CAPRI` | "Incorrect" | Failed docking classification |

These penalties apply when:
- A system is missing from the submission
- A required monomer type directory is absent
- No decoy models can be parsed
- Structure loading fails

The `--allow_missing` flag enables evaluation on partial submissions by applying these penalties to missing systems rather than raising an error.

Sources: [README.md:365-377]()

The evaluation harness produces multiple output files for result analysis:

```mermaid
        SUMMARY["summary_statistics.csv<br/>Aggregate metrics"]
        LEADERBOARD["leaderboard.csv<br/>Ranking-ready format"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Per-System Contents"
        SYS_ID["system_id"]
        MONOMER_TYPE["monomer_type"]
        MODEL_RANK["model_rank"]
        ALL_METRICS["iRMS, LRMS<br/>Fnat, DockQ<br/>CAPRI class"]
    end

        MEDIAN["Median metrics"]
        COVERAGE["System coverage %"]
    end
    
    PER_SYSTEM --> SYS_ID
    PER_SYSTEM --> MONOMER_TYPE
    PER_SYSTEM --> MODEL_RANK
    PER_SYSTEM --> ALL_METRICS
    
    SUMMARY --> METHOD
    SUMMARY --> SPLIT
    SUMMARY --> TOP_N
    SUMMARY --> MEDIAN
    SUMMARY --> COVERAGE
    
    PER_SYSTEM --> LEADERBOARD
    SUMMARY --> LEADERBOARD
    
    style PER_SYSTEM fill:#e1f5ff
    style SUMMARY fill:#fff4e1
    style LEADERBOARD fill:#ffe1f5
```

**Description**: The evaluation system generates granular per-system metrics for detailed analysis and aggregated summaries for method comparison. The leaderboard format follows community standards for result publication.

Sources: [README.md:380-381]()

## Test Set Selection

PINDER provides three benchmark test sets with different characteristics:

| Test Set | Systems | Purpose | Deleaking Strategy |
|----------|---------|---------|-------------------|
| **PINDER-XL** | 1,955 | Full evaluation benchmark | Structure & interface similarity |
| **PINDER-S** | 250 | Fast evaluation subset | Sampled from PINDER-XL |
| **PINDER-AF2** | 180 | AF2-MM comparison | iAlign-based transitive deleaking |

### Test Set Distribution

| Property | PINDER-XL | PINDER-S | PINDER-AF2 |
|----------|-----------|----------|------------|
| Holo pairs | 1,955 | 250 | 180 |
| Apo pairs | 342 | 93 | 30 |
| AF2 pairs | 1,747 | 250 | 127 |
| Heterodimers | - | 188 | - |
| Homodimers | - | 62 | - |

Each test set is stored in the `test_set_pdbs/` directory with native structures and pre-aligned monomers.

Sources: [README.md:244-252]()

**Description**: The evaluation system integrates with the full training-to-leaderboard pipeline. Models trained on PINDER-Train generate predictions on test sets, which are evaluated by `pinder_eval` to produce leaderboard-comparable results alongside reference methods.

Sources: [README.md:288-298]()

## Evaluation Best Practices

### System Coverage

For fair comparison on leaderboards:
1. Evaluate on complete test sets (all systems in PINDER-XL/S/AF2)
2. Report coverage percentage if submission is incomplete
3. Use `--allow_missing` flag for partial submissions (penalties applied)

### Monomer Type Selection

Match evaluation to training conditions:
- If trained on **holo monomers**: evaluate using `holo_decoys/`
- If trained on **apo monomers**: evaluate using `apo_decoys/`
- If trained on **predicted monomers**: evaluate using `predicted_decoys/`

### Performance Optimization

For large-scale evaluation:
1. Use `--max_workers` to control parallelism based on available resources
2. Pre-validate decoy directory structure before running evaluation
3. Consider PINDER-S for rapid iteration during development
4. Use PINDER-XL/AF2 for final leaderboard submission

### Result Interpretation

When analyzing results:
1. Check system coverage in summary statistics
2. Compare median metrics (more robust than mean for skewed distributions)
3. Examine top-N success rates (e.g., % of systems with acceptable prediction in top 10)
4. Review per-system results to identify failure modes
5. Compare against baseline physics-based methods (FroDock, HDock, PatchDock)

Sources: [README.md:288-298](), [README.md:365-377]()

## Python API Usage

The evaluation system can also be used programmatically:

```python
from pinder.eval.dockq import MethodMetrics
from pathlib import Path

# Initialize evaluation
evaluator = MethodMetrics(
    eval_dir=Path("./predictions/my_method"),
    method_name="my_method",
    split="test",
    subset="pinder_s"
)

# Run evaluation
results = evaluator.evaluate()

# Access aggregated metrics
summary = evaluator.get_summary_statistics()
leaderboard_entry = evaluator.get_leaderboard_row()

# Access per-system results
per_system_df = evaluator.per_system_metrics
```

This API provides the same functionality as the CLI with programmatic access to results for integration into larger pipelines or custom analysis workflows.

Sources: [README.md:378-381]()

# Page: Evaluation Harness

# Evaluation Harness

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



The evaluation harness provides a standardized framework for evaluating protein-protein docking methods on PINDER test sets. It processes predictions from docking methods and computes CAPRI-standard metrics to enable fair comparisons across different approaches.

For detailed information on the specific metrics calculated (iRMS, LRMS, Fnat, DockQ), see [Metrics](#6.2). For information on the available benchmark test sets, see [Benchmark Test Sets](#6.3).

## Overview

The evaluation harness accepts predictions organized in a standardized directory structure and produces evaluation results for one or more docking methods. It supports parallel processing, handles missing predictions with penalty scores, and can evaluate custom test sets beyond the standard PINDER splits.

The evaluation process consists of three main stages:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Input Stage"
        DECOYS["Predicted Decoys<br/>(PDB files)"]
        NATIVE["Native Structures<br/>(Ground truth)"]
        INDEX["Index/Metadata<br/>(Test set definitions)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing Stage"
        LOADER["DecoyLoader<br/>Load and validate decoys"]
        METRICS["MethodMetrics<br/>Calculate CAPRI metrics"]
        PARALLEL["Parallel Processing<br/>(multiprocessing)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Stage"
        CSV["Results CSV<br/>(Per-system metrics)"]
        SUMMARY["Summary Statistics<br/>(Aggregated results)"]
    end
    
    DECOYS --> LOADER
    NATIVE --> LOADER
    INDEX --> LOADER
    LOADER --> PARALLEL
    PARALLEL --> METRICS
    METRICS --> CSV
    CSV --> SUMMARY
```

**Sources:** [README.md:300-380]()

## CLI Tool: pinder_eval

The `pinder_eval` command-line tool is the primary interface for running evaluations. It orchestrates the entire evaluation workflow and provides flexible options for different use cases.

### Command Syntax

```bash
pinder_eval --eval_dir <path> [OPTIONS]
```

### Command-Line Options

| Option | Short | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `--eval_dir` | `-f` | string | Yes | Path to directory containing method predictions |
| `--serial` | `-s` | flag | No | Disable parallel processing (use single process) |
| `--method_name` | `-m`, `-n` | string | No | Custom name for output CSV file |
| `--allow_missing` | `-a` | flag | No | Allow missing systems without failing |
| `--custom_index` | `-c` | string | No | Path or GCS URI to custom index with alternative splits |
| `--max_workers` | `-w` | integer | No | Maximum number of parallel processes (default: all cores) |

### Usage Examples

Evaluate a single method with default settings:
```bash
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions/my_method/
```

Evaluate with custom method name and limited parallelism:
```bash
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions/my_method/ \
    --method_name "MyMethod-v2" \
    --max_workers 8
```

Evaluate custom test set allowing missing predictions:
```bash
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions/my_method/ \
    --custom_index ./my_custom_index.parquet \
    --allow_missing
```

**Sources:** [README.md:308-326]()

## Directory Structure Requirements

The evaluation harness expects a specific directory structure that organizes predictions by method, system ID, and monomer type.

### Standard Directory Layout

```mermaid
graph TD
    ROOT["eval_dir/"]
    METHOD["method_name/"]
    SYSTEM1["system_id_1/"]
    SYSTEM2["system_id_2/"]
    
    HOLO["holo_decoys/"]
    APO["apo_decoys/"]
    PRED["predicted_decoys/"]
    
    DECOY1["model_1.pdb"]
    DECOY2["model_2.pdb"]
    DECOY3["model_N.pdb"]
    
    ROOT --> METHOD
    METHOD --> SYSTEM1
    METHOD --> SYSTEM2
    
    SYSTEM1 --> HOLO
    SYSTEM1 --> APO
    SYSTEM1 --> PRED
    
    HOLO --> DECOY1
    HOLO --> DECOY2
    APO --> DECOY1
    APO --> DECOY2
    PRED --> DECOY1
    PRED --> DECOY2
    PRED --> DECOY3
```

### Concrete Example

```
eval_dir_example/
└── some_method/
    ├── 1an1__A1_P00761--1an1__B1_P80424/
    │   ├── apo_decoys/
    │   │   ├── model_1.pdb
    │   │   └── model_2.pdb
    │   ├── holo_decoys/
    │   │   ├── model_1.pdb
    │   │   └── model_2.pdb
    │   └── predicted_decoys/
    │       ├── model_1.pdb
    │       └── model_2.pdb
    └── 1b8m__A1_P23560--1b8m__B1_P34130/
        ├── holo_decoys/
        │   ├── model_1.pdb
        │   └── model_2.pdb
        └── predicted_decoys/
            ├── model_1.pdb
            └── model_2.pdb
```

### Directory Structure Components

| Component | Naming Convention | Description |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
| **Method Directory** | Any valid directory name | Top-level directory for a single docking method |
| **System Directory** | PINDER system ID format | Directory named with exact PINDER system ID (e.g., `1an1__A1_P00761--1an1__B1_P80424`) |
| **Decoy Type Directories** | `holo_decoys`, `apo_decoys`, `predicted_decoys` | Subdirectories for predictions using different monomer types |
| **Decoy Files** | Must match regex pattern | PDB files containing predicted complex structures |

**Sources:** [README.md:329-361]()

## Naming Conventions

### System ID Format

System IDs follow the PINDER convention:
```
<receptor>--<ligand>
```

Where each monomer follows:
```
<pdb_id>__<chain_id>_<uniprot_id>
```

Example: `1an1__A1_P00761--1an1__B1_P80424`

### Decoy File Naming

Decoy files must contain a rank number that can be extracted using the regex pattern: `r"\d+(?=\D*$)"` (implemented in `MethodMetrics`).

Valid naming patterns:
- `model_1.pdb`, `model_2.pdb`, ... (rank extracted: 1, 2, ...)
- `decoy_001.pdb`, `decoy_002.pdb`, ... (rank extracted: 1, 2, ...)
- `prediction_rank_5.pdb` (rank extracted: 5)

The rank determines the order in which predictions are evaluated, with lower ranks (e.g., 1) representing higher-confidence predictions.

### Chain Naming in Decoys

Each decoy PDB file must contain exactly two chains:
- Chain `R`: Receptor monomer
- Chain `L`: Ligand monomer

This convention ensures consistent alignment with native structures during metric calculation.

**Sources:** [README.md:360-362]()

## Evaluation Workflow

The evaluation harness processes predictions through a multi-stage pipeline that loads decoys, calculates metrics, and aggregates results.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "1. Discovery"
        SCAN["Scan eval_dir<br/>Find method directories"]
        IDENTIFY["Identify system IDs<br/>Validate structure"]
    end
    
    subgraph "2. Validation"
        CHECK_NATIVE["Load native structures<br/>from PINDER dataset"]
        CHECK_DECOYS["Validate decoy files<br/>Check chain IDs"]
        EXTRACT_RANK["Extract rank from<br/>filename (regex)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "3. Metric Calculation"
        ALIGN["Superpose decoy to native<br/>using PinderSystem"]
        IRMSD["Calculate interface RMSD"]
        LRMSD["Calculate ligand RMSD"]
        FNAT["Calculate fraction native<br/>contacts"]
        DOCKQ["Calculate DockQ score"]
        CAPRI["Assign CAPRI category"]
    end
    
    subgraph "4. Aggregation"
        PER_DECOY["Per-decoy metrics<br/>(all ranks)"]
        BEST["Best prediction metrics<br/>(rank 1 or best DockQ)"]
        SUMMARY["Summary statistics<br/>(mean, median, success rate)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "5. Output"
        WRITE_CSV["Write results CSV<br/>(one per method)"]
        WRITE_SUMMARY["Write summary statistics"]
    end
    
    SCAN --> IDENTIFY
    IDENTIFY --> CHECK_NATIVE
    CHECK_NATIVE --> CHECK_DECOYS
    CHECK_DECOYS --> EXTRACT_RANK
    EXTRACT_RANK --> ALIGN
    ALIGN --> IRMSD
    ALIGN --> LRMSD
    ALIGN --> FNAT
    IRMSD --> DOCKQ
    LRMSD --> DOCKQ
    FNAT --> DOCKQ
    DOCKQ --> CAPRI
    CAPRI --> PER_DECOY
    PER_DECOY --> BEST
    BEST --> SUMMARY
    SUMMARY --> WRITE_CSV
    WRITE_CSV --> WRITE_SUMMARY
```

**Sources:** [README.md:300-380]()

## Missing System Handling

When a method fails to produce predictions for a system in the test set, the evaluation harness applies penalty scores to enable fair comparison across methods.

### Penalty Scores

```python
{
    "iRMS": 100.0,
    "LRMS": 100.0,
    "Fnat": 0.0,
    "DockQ": 0.0,
    "CAPRI": "Incorrect",
}
```

### Behavior Modes

| Mode | CLI Flag | Behavior |
|------|----------|----------|
| **Strict** (default) | None | Evaluation fails if any system is missing from any test set split |
| **Lenient** | `--allow_missing` | Missing systems receive penalty scores; evaluation continues |

### Missing System Detection

The harness identifies missing systems by comparing:
1. System IDs present in the method's directory structure
2. System IDs defined in the test set split (from index)

For each missing system:
- A warning is logged
- Penalty scores are assigned if `--allow_missing` is enabled
- The method's aggregate statistics reflect the penalty

**Sources:** [README.md:365-376]()

## Code Components

The evaluation harness is implemented in the `pinder-eval` package with key components organized as follows:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "CLI Layer"
        MAIN["pinder_eval<br/>(CLI entry point)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Orchestration Layer"
        METHOD_METRICS["MethodMetrics<br/>pinder.eval.dockq.method"]
        EVAL_RUNNER["evaluate_methods<br/>pinder.eval.dockq.method"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Metric Calculation"
        DOCKQ_CALC["calculate_dockq<br/>pinder.eval.dockq"]
        RMSD_CALC["calculate_rmsd<br/>pinder.eval.dockq"]
        FNAT_CALC["calculate_fnat<br/>pinder.eval.dockq"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Data Loading"
        DECOY_LOADER["DecoyLoader<br/>Load PDB decoys"]
        SYSTEM_LOADER["PinderSystem<br/>Load native structures"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Utilities"
        STRUCTURE_OPS["Structure operations<br/>pinder.core.structure"]
        INDEX_OPS["Index operations<br/>pinder.core.index"]
    end
    
    MAIN --> METHOD_METRICS
    METHOD_METRICS --> EVAL_RUNNER
    EVAL_RUNNER --> DOCKQ_CALC
    EVAL_RUNNER --> RMSD_CALC
    EVAL_RUNNER --> FNAT_CALC
    EVAL_RUNNER --> DECOY_LOADER
    DECOY_LOADER --> SYSTEM_LOADER
    DOCKQ_CALC --> STRUCTURE_OPS
    RMSD_CALC --> STRUCTURE_OPS
    FNAT_CALC --> STRUCTURE_OPS
    METHOD_METRICS --> INDEX_OPS
```

### Key Classes and Functions

| Component | Location | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| `MethodMetrics` | `pinder.eval.dockq.method` | Orchestrates evaluation for a single method |
| `evaluate_methods` | `pinder.eval.dockq.method` | Evaluates multiple methods in parallel |
| `calculate_dockq` | `pinder.eval.dockq` | Computes DockQ score from individual metrics |
| `calculate_rmsd` | `pinder.eval.dockq` | Computes interface and ligand RMSD |
| `calculate_fnat` | `pinder.eval.dockq` | Computes fraction of native contacts |

**Sources:** [README.md:378-380]()

## Programmatic Usage

The evaluation harness can be used programmatically through the `pinder.eval` module, providing flexibility for custom workflows and integration into larger pipelines.

### Basic Programmatic Evaluation

```python
from pinder.eval.dockq import MethodMetrics

# Initialize evaluator for a single method
evaluator = MethodMetrics(
    method_name="my_docking_method",
    eval_dir="./predictions/",
    allow_missing=False,
    custom_index=None,
)

# Run evaluation
results = evaluator.evaluate()

# Access results
for system_id, metrics in results.items():
    print(f"{system_id}: DockQ={metrics['DockQ']:.3f}")
```

### Evaluating Multiple Methods

```python
from pinder.eval.dockq.method import evaluate_methods

# Evaluate all methods in directory
all_results = evaluate_methods(
    eval_dir="./predictions/",
    serial=False,  # Use parallel processing
    max_workers=8,
    allow_missing=True,
)

# Results organized by method name
for method, results in all_results.items():
    print(f"\n{method} Summary:")
    print(f"  Mean DockQ: {results['mean_dockq']:.3f}")
    print(f"  Success Rate: {results['success_rate']:.2%}")
```

### Custom Index Evaluation

```python
from pinder.eval.dockq import MethodMetrics

# Use custom test set
evaluator = MethodMetrics(
    method_name="my_method",
    eval_dir="./predictions/",
    custom_index="gs://my-bucket/custom_index.parquet",
)

results = evaluator.evaluate()
```

**Sources:** [README.md:378-380]()

## Output Format

The evaluation harness produces structured output files containing per-system metrics and summary statistics.

### Per-System Metrics CSV

Each evaluated method produces a CSV file with columns:

| Column | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `system_id` | string | PINDER system identifier |
| `monomer_type` | string | Type of monomer used (`holo`, `apo`, `predicted`) |
| `split` | string | Dataset split (`test`, `val`, or custom split name) |
| `rank` | integer | Prediction rank (1 = best) |
| `iRMS` | float | Interface RMSD (Å) |
| `LRMS` | float | Ligand RMSD (Å) |
| `Fnat` | float | Fraction of native contacts (0-1) |
| `DockQ` | float | DockQ score (0-1) |
| `CAPRI` | string | CAPRI category (`Incorrect`, `Acceptable`, `Medium`, `High`) |

### Summary Statistics

Aggregated statistics computed for each method and monomer type:

| Metric | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Mean DockQ | Average DockQ score across all systems |
| Median DockQ | Median DockQ score |
| Success Rate | Fraction of systems with acceptable or better predictions |
| High Quality Rate | Fraction of systems with high-quality predictions |
| Mean iRMS | Average interface RMSD |
| Mean LRMS | Average ligand RMSD |
| Mean Fnat | Average fraction of native contacts |

**Sources:** [README.md:300-380]()

## Performance Considerations

### Parallel Processing

By default, the evaluation harness uses all available CPU cores to process systems in parallel. This can be controlled with:

```bash
# Use 8 cores
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions/ --max_workers 8

# Use single process (for debugging)
pinder_eval --eval_dir ./predictions/ --serial
```

### Memory Usage

Memory usage scales with:
- Number of systems being evaluated
- Size of decoy structures
- Number of parallel workers

For large-scale evaluations (e.g., PINDER-XL with 1,955 systems), consider limiting `--max_workers` based on available RAM.

### Storage Requirements

Output files require minimal storage:
- Per-method CSV: ~1-10 MB depending on number of systems and decoys
- Summary statistics: <1 KB per method

**Sources:** [README.md:308-326]()
